subtopic: PENITENTIARIES
PENITENTIARIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on May 15, at the William Head Penitentiary near Victoria, B.C., Professor Douglas Ayers drew attention to an important change in public policy with respect to penitentiaries. He reminded Canadians that traditionally in our social policy one of the purposes of our penitentiaries is rehabilitation. We have never accepted the view that the sole purpose of a penitentiary is to punish, or to deter, or to hold people in custody. Reflecting our moral perspectives, we expect penitentiaries to try very hard to encourage, direct, and lead prisoners to responsible lives. The way we deal with our prisoners reflects the kind of people we are and the kind of society we wish to be.
The annual report of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) for 1981-82 defines the over-all mandate of the Correctional Service of Canada as being " . . . responsible for administering the sentences of the courts, as well as the decisions of the National Parole Board, affecting the release of offenders sentenced to two years or more". There is nothing in this statement even suggestive of rehabilitation. The June 6 article in Maclean's magazine by Val Ross suggests that in recent years the purposes of Canadian penitentiaries have been reformulated in such a way as to exclude that goal. Dr. Ayers pointed out that this is why the Solicitor General was so easily able to threaten to cancel the effective ten-year-old education program of the University of Victoria.
I would urge the Government to be unequivocal and to restore rehabilitation as one of the primary goals of the penitentiary system.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, every Canadian believes deeply in two principles-that his or her fellow Canadians are decent, honest and law abiding, and that those who would disrupt our system of peace, order and democratic Government should be found and dealt with. That
these two principles are sometimes difficult to reconcile is inevitable. But it is also true that, in reconciling them, balance must be steadfastly sought. For this reason, the comments of the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) yesterday, to the effect that nobody is exempt from security service scrutiny, are an affront to decent, thoughtful Canadians.
The Minister, who appears to be running for membership in George Orwell's "Animal Farm", has somehow lost sight of the first principle of justice in a free society, that is, that nobody should be the object of a security inquiry by the state without some reasonable evidence in the first place that a security risk may exist to justify the investigation.
Any Minister who accepts the view that all Canadians should be automatically and routinely suspect, that someone who is not guilty would not object to being investigated, that we, as loyal citizens, should bear the onus of proving our innocence, that Canadians should assume they are under scrutiny and behave accordingly-any such Minister has no place in office in this land and most certainly not in the office of Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a concern to me that many Canadians are not aware of the various disarmament initiatives in which Canada participates.
The most notable arms control negotiations currently under way are, first, the Intermediate Nuclear Force talks which are being held between the United States and the Soviet Union in Geneva, and second, the Strategic Arms Reduction talks in which the United States and the Soviet Union are debating the reduction of intercontinental ballistic missiles. Canada, as a member of NATO and NORAD, through our discussions with the United States, has an important say in these arms control negotiations.
Canada is a full participant in the mutual and balanced force reduction negotiations between NATO and the Warsaw Pact, which are looking at the number of troops and weapons that would be acceptable for each side in Europe.
In addition, Canada participates in the 35-nation conference on security and co-operation in Europe, which includes discussions on military matters such as confidence building measures between east and west European nations.
Canada also participates in the United Nations Disarmament Commission which meets year round in Geneva. Of special note for the current year is that Canada is chairman of the committee which is working toward a ban on all chemical and biological weapons.
In addition, Canada is one of the very few countries which has an official ambassador for disarmament.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, for over a decade military observers have viewed with alarm the deterioration of the Canadian Armed Forces. Personnel has
been reduced from a 1960 level of 126,000 to a current level of
80,000.	The reserves experienced an even greater reduction.
[DOT] (mo)
Much of the equipment used by the Canadian Armed Forces is now aged and obsolete, yet the officers and ranks struggle to meet our NATO and other commitments in defence of Canada and the free world. Promises of improvements and increased spending on national defence have not been kept. Now the Government must act.
The House of Commons has been silenced by the Government majority, but the report of the Senate subcommittee on National Defence has exposed the real facts on Maritime Command and defence policy to public view. We see a naval force crippled by inadequate equipment and stymied by lack of ministerial policy direction.
The subcommittee recommendations are detailed and thoughtful, and deserve careful examination by the Government. In broad terms, we must give force to the demand for a $550 million annual increase in the expenditures to arrest the decline in status and readiness of our Maritime forces. Such an increase would generate job-creation activity in shipbuilding, and more important, would stall the decline in conventional arms and minimize the need to resort to nuclear weapons in our national defence.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: UNITED STATES INVOLVEMENT IN CENTRAL AMERICA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in a speech to the United Nations Association in Ottawa the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) stressed Canada's opposition to armed attacks on legitimate Governments in Central America but remained silent on U.S. financed and directed attacks on Nicaragua. The Canadian Government has not demanded evidence of the existence of arms shipments from Nicaragua to Honduras which the U.S. says justifies its support for counter revolutionary activities in Honduras and Nicaragua. The Canadian Government has not condemned the U.S. program of "destabilization" of Nicaragua, a program which has brought about the death of over 700 Nicaraguans in the last six months. The Canadian Government has not challenged the U.S. campaign of disinformation about conditions in Nicaragua, and in particular the American distortion of the situtaion of the Miskito Indians.
Instead of silently backing U.S. policy in Central America, Canada should be moving forward to help Nicaraguans build a democratic, pluralistic and prosperous society as they approach the fourth anniversary of their revolution this July 19.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT
WESTERN GRAIN TRANSPORTATION ACT
subsubtopic: CALL FOR MEETING OF WESTERN MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT TO SUGGEST IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, surely by this time the Government must realize that western Canada does not want Bill C-155 in its present form. My idea of a democratic Government is that it endeavours to reflect the thinking of the people in its legislation and in its administration. If the Government would do that instead of telling the people what is good for them, as Bill C-155 does, it would call a meeting of the western Members of Parliament who represent the people of the West, and who are accountable to the people who elect them, and ascertain what has to be done to remove the major objections to the Bill.
For instance, why would the Government of Canada want to destroy the cattle and hog industry of western Canada? What changes to the Bill would have to be made to permit these industries to expand and reach their potential? Industrial development and manufacturing are required in the West. We have many raw materials and the expertise; why can we not invest and build up this industry? Surely in a country as large and as diverse as Canada there is room for development in both the West and the East. Let us start talking reasonably to each other with a view to permitting and encouraging the people of all parts of this great country to grow and play their part in building a greater Canada.
Forcing Bill C-155 on western Canada may appease the appetites for power but will, in the long run, be another nail in the coffin of Confederation. I love Canada and I do not want to see it broken up. Why can we not build this nation together, with all the regions of Canada playing their part?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the minister of Finance which concerns the 1.5 milion unemployed men and women who would still like to have jobs. subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER GROUND CF-104 STARFIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on May 24 I asked the Minister of National Defence whether he would consider grounding the Starfighters because of their unacceptably high attrition rate. He replied:
Madam Speaker, if there were any unreasonable risk in letting our pilots fly any of our planes I would stop them from flying right away.
According to press reports the Minister has stated that he will not ground the fighter but will temporarily curtail certain operational exercises. In view of yesterday's accident, will the Minister not now completely ground the Starfighters until the causes of the crashes are known and, possibly, rectified?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER GROUND CF-104 STARFIGHTER AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I mentioned yesterday, after the news of the crash in Germany reached me I had a conversation with the Chief of Defence Staff and the Director of Air Command. I asked them for their opinions. They advised me there was no serious reason just because of the accident to ground the aircraft. They indicated that most of the maintenance and safety precautions with respect to the aircraft are at the highest level they have ever been. They also advised me that only 15 per cent of the accidents that have occurred in the last 15 years of flying these planes were due to mechanical defects. The remainder were not as a result of mechanical defects.
Also, as a precaution, the Chief of Defence Staff yesterday issued an order at my suggestion that some of the air to ground exercises will be suspended until we have the reasons for the last two crashes. According to the Chief of Defence Staff at Air Command there was no serious reason why we should ground the aircraft.
Yesterday was a very bad day. Two Jaguar aircraft from the British Air Force crashed in Goose Bay. That was not a reason, again, to ground these aircraft just because these accidents happened. These Jaguar planes were also old. They are to be replaced by the Tornado, probably next year.
Just because there are crashes and even though we know the reasons for these crashes, we do not think that these reasons call for us to ground them.

It could be human error. The statistics are there.
Maybe I should mention, Madam Speaker, that following these accidents, I, of course, sent my condolences to the Minister of Defence for Germany, and I received his reply today. I want to quote his concluding sentence. It reads as follows:

speechtext:

It has to do with the visit of their Royal Highnesses to Parliament Hill next Monday. Will the Deputy Prime Minister take steps to remove the eyesore that is next to the Centennial Flame on the direct access route to the Centre Block in order that Canadians might perceive their Royal Highnesses on television via pictures taken from the platforms erected directly opposite that eyesore?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the high-flying Minister of State for International Trade. It concerns the implementation of the report of the auto task force and the fact that the voluntary agreement with the Japanese on the import of Japanese
June 17, 1983

automobiles expires on July 1. Could the Minister give us a commitment that in his talks with the Japanese about the importation of Japanese cars he will try to negotiate the recommendations of this task force so that there will be Canadian content in the Japanese cars which Canadians will want to buy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subtopic: AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY
subsubtopic: CANADIAN CONTENT IN JAPANESE MANUFACTURED AUTOMOBILES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his very pertinent and timely question. I want to say to him that the negotiations with the Japanese in relation to a further period of restraint are continuing and that I would be hopeful of having in place, by July 1, an arrangement which would cover a restraint level until the end of the fiscal year, next March 31. If that is not the case, then I would propose other action to Cabinet prior to July 1, 1983.
In relation to the recommendations of the task force, I think the manner in which that must be approached is that we get into place an agreed level of restraint from now until March 31, and that we take advantage of that time period for the distinguished Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, in co-operation of course with the Department of Trade, to see to it that negotiations with the Japanese on the question of content go forth pursuant to examination by Cabinet of the recommendations of the task force.

subtopic: CANADIAN CONTENT IN JAPANESE MANUFACTURED TRUCKS
CANADIAN CONTENT IN JAPANESE MANUFACTURED TRUCKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question also concerns the task force. The principal recommendations of the task force are really very similar to the 1965 Auto Pact with the United States that called for Canadian content for the production of American cars in this country. It is really a fair play document that is expanding the same rules to other companies in other countries.
1 would like to ask the Minister, in light of the fact that the importation of Japanese trucks has gone up by 54 per cent over last year in the first quarter of this year, is he including the importation of Japanese trucks as part of his talks with the Japanese. Would he like to see the same rules of Canadian content apply to trucks as the report of the task force says should apply to both trucks and cars? Would he also negotiate for Canadian content in trucks as well?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald Regan (Minister of State (International Trade)):
subtopic: CANADIAN CONTENT IN JAPANESE MANUFACTURED TRUCKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, trucks are, of course, part of the automotive trade between our countries and provide jobs in the same way as do cars. While the Japanese have historically been reluctant to include trucks in any arrangement for restraint, that is a subject of discussions that are taking place.
1 want to point out to the low-flying Hon. Member that there are two factors which I consider to be very hopeful at the present time. The first is that the market for cars is improving substantially this year as recovery from the recession takes place. The other is that there seems to be a growing indication
Oral Questions
that North American automobiles are becoming more competitive in the eyes of the public. I see a pattern of recovery coming about in the choice of North American cars over imported cars.
We are watching the situation in relation to trucks very closely and we are concerned about the number of trucks that have been sold. That is a matter for examination along with the matter of automobiles.

1.	Is the Economic Council of Canada's econometric model capable of estimating the impact on short-term and long-term interest rates in Canada for varying levels of the deficit and, if so, what changes in short-term and long-term interest rates from current levels does it predict based on the deficit projections contained in the Budget?
2.	What impact would the changes in interest rates have on the cost of servicing the national debt?

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
1. (a) The Economic Council of Canada econometric model is capable of estimating the impact on short-term and long-term interest rates in Canada for varying levels of the deficit. Depending on the factors that cause the deficit to vary some judgments are necessary when using the econometric model to estimate such impacts. These judgments are related to channels of influence that the econometric model, in its general form, does not account for when used in a specific application.
(b) Imposing, among other things, our best judgment about the path of interest rates in the United States, the most recent national accounts revisions and the April 19, 1983 federal budget, on the econometric model of the Economic Council of Canada, annual averages of short-term interest rates in Canada in the medium run will remain unchanged from current levels; annual averages of long-term interest rates in the medium run continue a downward trend.
2. in the absence of any change in spending levels the cost of servicing the national debt and interest rates are positively related. For example, see Table A-2 of The Fiscal Plan, April 19, 1983, The Federal Budget. In Table A-2 the impact of reducing interest rates by 100 basic points is reported. Such a reduction would reduce the deficit by $1.4 billion. A similar result has been obtained using the econometric model of the Economic Council of Canada.

subtopic: OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSIONS' REPORTS RESPECTING NOVA SCOTIA AND SASKATCHEWAN

speechtext:
The House proceeded to the consideration of objections to the reports of the Electoral Boundaries Commissions for the Provinces of Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan.
Electoral Boundaries

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: OBJECTIONS TO COMMISSIONS' REPORTS RESPECTING NOVA SCOTIA AND SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise in a representative capacity on behalf of my colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party from the Province of Nova Scotia to indicate our objection to the report of the Electoral Boundaries Commission for the Province of Nova Scotia.
We appreciate and recognize that it is always a difficult task to settle what must be, in the final analysis, an arbitrary decision, but at the same time there are methods and processes that can be followed to bring about a proper distribution that will be satisfactory to the greatest number of persons.
Let me begin by recognizing that the point of the exercise is to ensure the representation of people, in this case people in the Province of Nova Scotia, in the Parliament of Canada. It is for that reason that we want to be extremely careful that the process results in a fair and adequate representation.
Let me provide some background to this process, Mr. Speaker. Under the provisions of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act we implement those provisions that were enshrined in the British North America Act, now called the Constitution Act, that were intended to ensure proper representation for Canadians as time went on. The method for ensuring such representation was to provide for a decennial census. This census began in 1871 and has continued every tenth year thereafter. It was on the basis of the results of that count of the population that we determined the representation in the House of Commons.
Nova Scotia has not always fared well in this process. In 1867, at the time of Confederation, the Province was one of the key members of the Confederation. Over the years the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec developed at a much greater rate and, in the result, Nova Scotia tended to pale in comparison to the major Provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Now there is rapid development in the West in the Provinces of British Columbia and Alberta and Nova Scotia assumes a relatively lower level role in our Confederation.
All of this has been taken into account in the process. It is now part of the process that Provinces are classified for electoral representation purposes as larger Provinces; other Provinces fall into the category of small Provinces. Nova Scotia falls into the small Province category.
I point that out because we in Nova Scotia believe that we are at our minimum level of representation. In fact, according to the floor rule for parliamentary representation, Nova Scotia cannot go below a level of ten Members of Parliament, that being the level equal to the number of seats provided for Nova Scotia in the other place.

June 17, 1983
Electoral Boundaries
In reviewing the history of this, I want to point out that on two occasions in the recent past, as a result of the 1941 census and as a result of the 1961 census, Nova Scotia has lost representation. Prior to the 1961 redistribution, Nova Scotia had 12 seats in the Parliament of Canada; as a result of the 1961 census, Nova Scotia was reduced to 11 parliamentary seats.
The proposal now before the House and represented by the work of the Commission under the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act would restore Nova Scotia to 12 seats. In a sense, the Province stands to gain by this process. The important point is to ensure that the gain is properly distributed over the population within the Province.
That brings me to the basis for our objection, Mr. Speaker. We do not consider that the work done by the Electoral Boundaries Commission in Nova Scotia, however adequate it was, should be approved without reflection of the kinds of criticisms we have raised. We have done that specifically in our objection which is part of the records of the House of Commons.
We believe that the Commission failed to give adequate attention and consideration to geographical, political and demographic factors when planning the distribution of electoral boundaries.
My second point, Mr. Speaker, is that the Commission included Sable Island in the constituency of Halifax. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), has a very special interest in that aspect of the redistribution; I am sure he will want to speak to that subject as this debate continues.
The third listed reason, Mr. Speaker, is that the Commission did not give adequate consideration to all the representations made to the Commission during the course of its public hearings.
I will begin, Mr. Speaker, with a consideration of the last point. There was very little in the way of public representation made to the Commission when it held its hearings across Nova Scotia. In fact, in some cases the hearings were cancelled because of lack of interest.
To put that matter in context, let me point out to the House of Commons that in the case of Nova Scotia the quotient which was used to determine the population base for each of the 12 constituencies was 70,620. Under the rules and regulations which apply to this redistribution process, that number can be varied by 25 per cent either way, that is, a minimum of 25 per cent below, which is a population of 52,965, and a maximum of 25 per cent above, which would result in a population of 88,275.
I believe the next step, Mr. Speaker, is to review the actual setting up of the 12 constituencies in relation to that population base, and what we find in terms of public objections which we feel were not given proper consideration. First of all, in those constituencies where there was no change in the boundaries and where, in fact, the population base was relatively
close to the mean of 70,600-that would include the federal constituency of South Shore and the federal constituency of South West Nova-there were, naturally enough, no real objections. I feel that pertains as well to the federal constituency of Cumberland-Colchester which was unchanged with a population base of 78,455. There were no objections. I believe the area of objection, Mr. Speaker, centers in the Halifax district where there now exists under the present electoral representation three federal constituencies within the County of Halifax. Under the changes which are proposed by the Electoral Boundaries Commission for Nova Scotia, there will be four constituencies, almost exactly within that same area. It is in fact Halifax County, plus a portion of Hants County.
It is understandable, therefore, that the majority of the objections would arise in relation to this change in the Halifax area whereby three federal constituencies are being expanded into four. I will deal with that in a more direct way and I am sure my colleague, the Hon. Member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, will want to make some remarks on the effects this has on his constituency, which will become the constituency of Dartmouth, and on the failure to include Sable Island within the constituency of Dartmouth.
I would like very briefly to comment on the federal constituencies for the Province of Nova Scotia. First of all, we have the constituency of Annapolis Valley-Hants, which has been well represented by my hon. colleague in the Progressive Conservative Party for over 18 years now. There has been very little change in the population base. After what little adjustments have been made it will be 72,174.
Cape Breton-East Richmond, which is a constituency the representation of which has fluctuated from party to party over the years, will have a population base of 64,495, which is a substantial 6,000 below the mean. However, there does not appear to be any special reasons for including territorial areas in that constituency beyond what are now part of the existing boundaries.
Cape Breton Highlands-Canso has a population base which has not changed. The population base is 65,883. Of course, we don't want that to change because the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) has enough difficulty getting around the constituency as it now is, and to provide the services which we all provide in our constituencies. Therefore, we do not want to see the people of Cape Breton Highlands-Canso be any less served than they are now. Therefore, we are not going to raise any special objection. Because of the fact that that is one of the smaller constituencies, no attempt has been made to enlarge it.
Cape Breton-The Sydneys involves the industrial community of the Sydneys and the surrounding area. It has a population base of 65,000. I would have to have some concern for my colleague who represents that constituency because it has a great deal of difficulty, mostly based on economic policies of the Government and the failure to provide adequate assistance for the Cape Breton steel industry-Sydney Steel Company-
June 17, 1983

which is a large employer in that area. Again, there cannot be real objection to the relatively low number of persons which form the population base in that constituency because it will provide sufficient difficulties for the Hon. Member who represents it. I know that Hon. Member is having quite a bit of difficulty at the present time.
The fifth constituency of Central Nova is well represented. Of course, the seat has now been declared vacant and we are anticipating a by-election there. We anticipate the continued good representation for that constituency by not only a member of the Progressive Conservative Party, but by the newly-elected Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party who, we understand, intends to run in the constituency of Central Nova. Under the adjustment process, that constituency would have a population base similar to Cape Breton Highlands-Canso and Cape Breton-The Sydneys of 65,332. Cumberland-Colchester is the sixth constituency and it will remain unchanged, along with South Shore and South West Nova, which are the eleventh and twelfth numbered constituencies, and they have not created any great difficulty in this process.
The new proposed constituencies are as follows: No. 7, Dartmouth; No. 8, Halifax; No. 9, Halifax East; and No. 10, Halifax West. Those are the four constituencies which are in the greater Halifax-Dartmouth area and are the constituencies with which we have the greatest complaint.
In the case of Halifax West, if that constituency had been left alone to include my own area of Clayton Park, the very place in which 1 live, it would have had a population almost exactly similar to the constituency of Halifax. For some strange reason, however, which I have yet to understand, the Boundaries Commission took the area of Clayton Park, where 1 live and where my children go to school, and where we patronize the local grocery store, lifted it out of Halifax West and plumped it down alongside Halifax, which is represented by my colleague, if not my friend, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan). In the result, instead of each constituency having the mean number of 70,6000, the federal constituency of Halifax ends up with a population base of 78,231 and Halifax West ends up with a population base of 68,676. If the location of Clayton Park in Halifax West had been left alone, the two constituencies would have been almost equal in population base. 1 feel it is kind of a strange thing-I am sure even my Liberal colleagues would agree-when they lift my very residence out of Halifax West and put it down in Halifax, resulting in an imbalance of population of some
10,000.	There is a difference now of 10,000. Halifax West has a population of 68,676 versus Halifax with a populaton of 78,231.
One of our concerns in this process must be the allegation of gerrymandering of constituencies. Of course, that immediately comes to mind when virtually your own house is moved from one place to another. However, I do not suspect that at all because I know that the honourable persons who served on the Electoral Boundaries Commission would not do something like that. 1 know Mr. Justice Pace, who represented the Liberal Party so well in the House of Assembly in Nova Scotia, would not do anything like that. I know Mr. O'Coyne who worked
Electoral Boundaries
and toiled so hard for the Liberal Party as an executive officer, or in some other capacity, would not think of doing a thing like that. I would not at all suggest that there would be any chicanery involved in this process, so I do not want to object any further to the removal of my own house and property from the constituency of Halifax West. I know the Minister of State for International Trade will not be there the next time around and I will not have to worry about that too much.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, let me just say that we are concerned that everyone in Nova Scotia receive adequate representation as a result of this process. We appreciate the fact that, as a result of the process, which incidentally increased the number of seats in the House of Commons from 282 to 310, Nova Scotia will get one more seat, an increase from 11 to 12, which will bring it back to the 1961 level. There are some benefits but we are concerned that the process is fairly and properly conducted. We have concern that the process was less than entirely adequate, with all due respect to the persons who applied the process and with all due regard for the fact that it is not a perfect process.
I want to give my colleague, the Hon. Member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East, the opportunity to contribute to this debate because I know he has some special concerns with respect to his own constituency, particularly with respect to the inclusion of Sable Island within the boundaries of the new constituency of Dartmouth.

Mr. Speaker, I wish we had more time in debates like this. There are a lot of Members from Saskatchewan who would like to speak in this particular debate about the report of the Saskatchewan Boundaries Commission in 1983. My good friend from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) is in the House. I know he would like to speak and I am sure he will later on. There are other Members of our Party who want to speak as well.
We had three very distinguished gentlemen on the Saskatchewan Commission which held hearings throughout the Province, Mr. Speaker, but 1 want to say, with respect, that I think they did not listen very well to many of the representations made to them by representatives of all three political Parties in Saskatchewan, members of which I think would concur in that statement.
Many of the hearings were very well attended. We had many ordinary citizens who came out to many of these hearings. We had representatives of all three political Parties who concurred on a number of things. We had the concurrence of the Saskatchewan MPs in the Conservative Party, which is half the Province, or seven, and the New Democratic Party, which is the other half, or seven, on many of the boundaries. Despite this harmony, this commonality, concerning what we thought should happen, in many cases the Commission did not listen to us or the people. For that reason we decided to file the objection we are now discussing in the House.

June 17, 1983
Electoral Boundaries
I want to stress at the outset that many of the things said to the Commission were said by representatives of all three political Parties and because of historical community interests and traditions in Saskatchewan. The point that really puzzled a lot of us in Saskatchewan is that the Boundaries Commission did not make very much use at all of the plus or minus 25 per cent rule. They drew arbitrary lines in many cases for our 14 Saskatchewan constituencies. They did not deviate from an average. For example, the least populous riding as recommended by them, to be called Regina-Lumsden, has a population of 67,183. The most populous riding is called Saskatoon-Dun-durn, which is primarily city but also partly rural, with a population of 71,432. So of the 14 ridings in Saskatchewan the difference between the least and the most populous will be 4,549 people. Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is good enough.
1 have had a chance to look at Boundary Commission reports from other Provinces and I notice that in many other Provinces the Commission has, in my opinion, more wisely interpreted the Act by making sure that the deviation is greater for sparsely populated and remote areas. The population will be larger for the urban centres. This was not done in Saskatchewan where a lot of the boundaries are very arbitrary. It is almost as if they took a calculator and divided our population into 14, then took a ruler and put it on the provincial census map and drew 14 areas. 1 do not think that is good enough. We should go back to the drawing board in Saskatchewan and come up with a map that the people of our Province want, one that will reflect the reality, the community interests, the history and traditions of Saskatchewan in a way which has been done many times in the past, and in other Provinces by Boundaries Commissions in the last few months.
To be specific, Mr. Speaker, the Commission ignored some of the guiding principles in planning redistribution, mainly the recognition of a community of interest. I can go over a number of these, and the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain could do the same thing, where that community of interests was often ignored by the Boundaries Commission. They wanted to have a more exact population figure in each riding, ignoring many times the community of interests.
The second principle they often ignored was the need to follow geographical patterns and boundaries. There is an excellent example of that in that part of the Province represented by myself and the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, namely the Qu'Appelle River Valley. The Qu'Appelle River is a natural geographical boundary and a natural community boundary. It is a natural boundary in so many ways historically in our Province yet that was ignored. In addition, the Commission did not agree to make as few changes as possible to establish ridings. That is spelled out in Subsection 13(b), Subsection 13(c)(1) and Subsection 13(c)(2) of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and is included in the terms of reference of the Commission. They did not follow the principle of community interests, geographical patterns and that of making as few changes as possible.
One can go over the map specifically. The map I have before me will create a brand new riding called Prince Albert-Churchill River. That riding, believe it or not, takes up over half of our Province geographically. Yet despite its massive
size that constituency has 68,132 people living in it, according to the census. We have many northern ridings in this country with small populations because they are remote, small communities, difficult to serve and with special interests and special needs. In this particular riding there are some 27,000 people who live in the north. They are lumped in with the environs of the City of Prince Albert in one particular constituency. If they wanted to recommend the creation of a northern constituency similar to some of the other Provinces or the Territories of this country, they could have recommended a special Act of this Parliament where we could create a northern riding that would have less than the minimum population. Or, Mr. Speaker, they could have used the plus or minus 25 per cent rule and create a riding which was much smaller in northern Canada. But they ignored this.
In our two big cities, Regina and Saskatoon, they once again ignored the community of interests. What they should have been doing was creating urban ridings because of the commonness of the community sense, or the community feeling. Because the two cities are now too large for just two urban ridings in each of the cases, what they should have done is what has been done time and time again in our Province and other Provinces, federally and provincially. They should have taken the overflow and the new suburbs and placed them into the most relevant rural ridings which touch the city boundaries. However, that was not done.
In the case of the city of Regina, they should have created two urban seats, placing the new suburbs on the east side of the city, into the Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain constituency, and, on the western side of Regina, placing the new suburbs in the south end of the city, Albert Park and other areas south of Waskana Creek. They should have put those into the Assiniboia riding to raise its population, so that we could have saved Assiniboia, which will disappear, by the way, for the first time ever if the new map comes into effect, a historical name and riding which the people in the Province want to keep and deserve to keep. By the way, it is not our riding now, it is a Conservative riding. However, this is one way of doing it.
Farmers in those rural communities would still have had their own constituency and some of the new suburbs of Regina, which are bordering on the riding, in the riding to give them adequate population. The people and the City of Regina would have had two totally urban constituencies, and that sense of history and tradition which is so important would have been guarded and preserved.
The same is true in the City of Saskatoon. Once again, we have a recommendation of three urban/rural ridings: part rural, part urban, part rural, part urban, part rural and part urban. That is not good enough. I do not think that reflects what our people want at all. Again, we could have had two strictly urban constituencies, placing some of the new suburbs into the adjoining rural riding of Humboldt-Lake Centre to
June 17, 1983

bring up its population and to preserve it, placing some of the new suburbs in the west end of Saskatoon into the adjoining riding of Kindersley, and that riding would have then been adequate in terms of numbers as well.
These are some specific examples of where the Commission did not listen to the people, where the Commission did not follow the history, precedent and practice of other Boundary Commissions, federal and provincial, over the years. 1 mentioned Assiniboia. This historical riding will disappear. There is also a boundary change in Swift Current-Maple Creek but, again, I think that this is going in the wrong way. A boundary change for Swift Current-Maple Creek could have been reached north of the South Saskatchewan River, as has occurred in the past-and I want to underline that-rather than moving the boundary substantially toward the east, which means eliminating Assiniboia in the process and creating all kinds of contortions in southeastern Saskatchewan as well. If it would have moved the boundary north, the boundary would have been where it has been in the past, and that would have been much less confusing for the citizens of that part of the country.
In my own constituency of Yorkton-Melville, I believe the Commission erred in both the northern and southern boundaries of the riding. Our part of the Province is one which has two natural boundaries. We have the Qu'Appelle River, the Qu'Appelle River Valley to the south. As Saskatchewan Members like the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) and others know, that is a natural boundary. There are school board divisions where, in the south, people are in a different school board than those in the north. Wheat pools are divided by the river, municipalities are divided by the river, and all kinds of community activities, church groups and so on are divided by the river. Instead, the Commission ignores the fact that this is a natural geographical, community, social, cultural and historical boundary and tries to put people on both sides of it into the same constituency.

In fact, there are people from communities in the southwest part of the new proposed Yorkton-Melville riding who never go to Yorkton and Melville to shop. They go into Regina to shop because it is much closer. That is where they always go for their social activities, or else they go into the eastern towns of Indian Head, Wolseley, Moosomin, Whitewood, or down toward Weyburn. Their sense of community is in that direction or in the direction of the City of Regina, and not north and east a long, long ways into the City of Yorkton.
I would like to mention the second natural boundary. Again, the Commission ignored the advice of ordinary citizens and folk, I suggest from all political Parties. I say this in response to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) who asks "Is it bad?" The Minister can check with Mr. Ralph Goodale, if he wishes.
Electoral Boundaries
In the north, we have a forest reserve. It is a natural boundary. It is natural because it is a big forest. People very seldom go through the forest reserve because all their organizations, communities and so on are to the south or, north of the reserve, to the north and to the west. It is a forest reserve where there are bears and other animals. However, people see that as being a natural boundary and that was said time and time again to the Commission. In fact, two members of the Commission on their way to Yorkton for the hearings drove through the forest reserve. They said they understood that this was a natural boundary because of the fact that they had just driven through it and they had seen what a forest reserve is really like; yet the map ignores this very natural boundary in northeastern Saskatchewan.
I do not know why these Commissions do not listen to ordinary folk. There is much more common sense in the minds of ordinary citizens of this country, it seems at times, than there is in the minds of people who are appointed to high positions by various Governments across the land.
I mention the constituency of Humboldt-Lake Centre, represented by my friend who is here in the House today. In the new map, this constituency disappears altogether. It is going, I believe, into five different constituencies. Right now that constituency which, I suppose, was historically called the old Lake Centre riding, represented by a former Prime Minister, John Diefenbaker, is one which was basically carved out of central Saskatchewan, the great grain producing area. There is commonness of interest, I suppose among those people who live between Prince Albert and Regina and Saskatoon, those who live in the central part of the Province. That riding, too, will disappear, going off into five different constituencies.
One way of saving the riding would have been to add some of the new suburbs of the City of Saskatoon, from the south eastern part of the City of Saskatoon, to Humboldt-Lake Centre. That would have raised its population very well.

One always trades off something. The populations are not large enough to create three fully urban ridings, but they can create 2.5 urban ridings. Instead of creating six urban ridings between the two cities, this way there would be four which were urban and two which were urban and rural. That would give a greater sense of community. In any event, that was the feeling of so many people in the Province from all the different political Parties.

June 17, 1983
Electoral Boundaries
Therefore, where do we go from here? I hope we can persuade those involved in the process from here on in that we should go back to the drawing board and listen to the ordinary folk in order that we might make greater use of the plus or minus 25 per cent rule, which has been done in Quebec and other Provinces, such as Ontario. Some of our rural areas have smaller populations because they are a little more scattered and remote at the north. If we are to have only one riding there should be a smaller population because of the fact that it is also remote. The urban centres, because they are more compact, could perhaps have slightly larger ridings or populations. Perhaps even a riding like mine, which is rural and urban now but where the towns are closer together and the farms are a little bit smaller, could be on the larger side as well. Those kinds of suggestions make sense.
Another matter which arose in our hearings concerns the fact that Saskatchewan has certain ethnic patterns, cultural patterns, in terms of where people live. This is another factor which was ignored by the Commission as it sat down and arbitrarily drew 14 lines on the map of our Province without anywhere near the regard it should have had for the reality concerning the Province.
One can also say that the riding of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake changes quite drastically as well. It is interesting once again to note that representatives of both political Parties that have MPs in that area were in agreement that the proposed boundaries by the Commission did not make any sense. In this case, they made some boundary changes but a change that was not recommended by either. I do not know where they get their ideas.
With that, I look forward to hearing other Members of the Saskatchewan delegation from both our Party and the Conservative Party try to persuade the powers that be that we have a map that reflects what the people of Saskatchewan really want and need.

Mr. Speaker, I am aware that there are only ten minutes left. I also know that the presentation on Nova Scotia was only half completed; the other half will be completed later.
1 will reduce my remarks to approximately five minutes since they correspond in many ways with those of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). I will put it very clearly to the House that the problem in Saskatchewan is basically that we have 4 per cent of the population of Canada and 35 per cent of the roads. The roads are our main communication technique.
The Commission has held to the view of the nineteenth century concept that one person should get one vote, or representation by population. To hold to that view realistically forced Parliament to introduce new legislation 25 years ago that used the word "may". While the British North America Act provides for keeping a provincial average, the legislation gave the Commission power to vary them up or down 25 per
cent based on two reasons which were geography and community of interest. The previous speaker has already referred to that. Therefore I want to keep my remarks confined to a simple part of the problem which was dealt with by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville. Simply, it is southern Saskast-chewan.
The community of interest can only be appreciated by those who must live and work there. I come from a riding south of Qu'Appelle where the boundary line has always been that river along which we have always moved back and forth in an easterly direction. It is a historic riding from where Members of Parliament have been sent to Ottawa since 1882, long before Saskatchewan was a Province. We call ourselves the mainliners because the main line of the CPR runs through our constituency and because the Trans-Canada Highway runs through it now.
The mainliners are from a cultural community that moves towards Regina east from west. Melville has east and west connections to Regina and Yorkton has east and west connections partially to Regina and partially to Saskatoon. For any map to meet the geographic conditions of Saskatchewan, it must allow for these features of geography.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville talked about a big forest barring one part of his riding from another. I talked about the Moose Mountains that are a barrier to us in the south. The point I am making is that the historic seat of Qu'Appelle has been cut into four parts. It certainly smashes a 100-year-old tradition and breaks the hearts of those people who went there from Quebec, Ontario, the Atlantic Provinces and all over the world. We have kept it as a community and to see it broken apart is a very dreadful experience for those who must endure it.
In my submission which I intend to send to the Commission, I have proposed more precise maps based on municipal boundaries, based on the barriers and based on the community of interest. This helps the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville by putting the natural boundary of Qu'Appelle between us and ties up the highways from Melville and Yorkton running north and west right through an area that he knows well since it was part of the seat he represented when he first came here. Those people move up and down that line. It is based on highways and the geographic boundaries.
The five constituencies which I believe I have mentioned in my representation are Yorkton, Melville and Regina, Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, and Swift Current. I put this proposal forward to the Commission in the form of maps. While they have seen those maps before, they did not listen properly and I hope that this time they will seriously consider these boundary adjustments for which all Parties made strong representations in the eight meetings we had last fall on these boundary adjustments. When we have all parties in Saskatchewan agreeing, that is news.
I am simply suggesting that the Commission pay attention to what the people who have to work in the fields and with others are trying to recommend. I have suggested minor changes as well. I will conclude my remarks and hope that the
June 17, 1983

House will take kindly to the representations we have made so that the Commission is impressed by the fact that Parliament does not like being confronted with actions which are different from what Parliament has directed this Commission to follow.

Mr. Speaker, I will also be relatively brief since 1 believe there are only about four minutes left. I wish to make three points. First, 1 am rapidly coming to the view that perhaps this Chamber might be well advised to express its sincere appreciation to the distinguished Commissioners and ask them to retire so that the House itself could undertake this job. I am coming to that view for a variety of reasons. The principal view is that I strongly believe that Members of this Chamber, as it exists on June 17 of 1983, are quite capable of rendering that type of representation which is required for the people of this country. I suggest that enlarging the House from its present 282 Members to approximately 312 Members is a burden on the taxpayers of Canada. It costs approximately $550,000 in taxpayers' money to keep each one of us here and support us with the variety of services that we require as matters become more technical in nature.
The fact of the matter is that when 1 came here I represented approximately 240,000 people. We did not have telephones. I was not able to fly home every weekend. Members had secretaries whom they called up from a pool and who were kind enough to type letters for us. By and large correspondence with our constituents was handwritten. It worked well. speakeroldname: Hon. Serge Joyal (Secretary of State) moved
subtopic: CANADA STUDENT LOANS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-161, an Act to amend the Canada Student Loans Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole, with the unanimous consent of the House.
He said: Mr. Speaker, upon rising today to resume debate on this Bill, I would like to express my gratitude to my colleagues on the other side of the House.

I want to thank all Members on both sides of the House for their co-operation, and especially the Ministers of Education in Canada who have co-operated with the Canadian Government in past months to achieve the proposed amendments that we will be debating today.

The Canada Student Loans program was established in 1964 and, since that time, has benefited about two million students. In 1980, an in-depth study was made of the various federal and provincial programs providing student assistance, and it was found that the vast majority of students, parents and the general public supported the basic principles underly-
26496

June 17, 1983
Canada Student Loans Act (No. 2) ing current student assistance programs. We are aware, however, that after twenty years, it is time to change some of the plan's basic elements to allow for rising costs of higher education and the socio-economic climate confronting the student today. The changes we are proposing involve additional funding of $60 million, to be paid over two years. In my view, these changes should not be seen as just amendments to a specific piece of legislation but as one of the basic elements of a broader objective, which is to make education accessible to all Canadian students and to maximize development of human resources.
My colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), has established a national training program which includes the Skill Growth Fund and the Critical Trade Skills Training Program. In addition, the Minister of State for Economic Development and the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston) has been collaborating with other Ministers on improving the direction and structure of research and technology development, especially in terms of the joint effort being made in this area by Government, industry and the academic world.
These initiatives and others of a similar nature, to which will be added the proposed changes in the Canada Student Loans Act, are all part of a group of proposals that reflect the changing character of higher education and of our economy. [English]
I would now like to indicate to the House the three main concerns which are addressed in Bill C-161 and to explain their importance to Canadian students.
The first concern pertains to loan limits. The present weekly loan limit is $56.25, a limit which was based on a previous annual limit of $1,800 set in 1974. We know that a 1983 dollar and a 1974 dollar do not have the same purchasing power, hence the need for an upward revision in the loan limit. The Bill now before the House proposes increasing the weekly loan limit from $56.25 to $100 a week, with some provision for escalation as required.
The Bill also takes into account the needs of students pursuing long-term studies. It is obvious, for example, that students pursuing medicine, law or post-graduate studies will require loans over a longer period than students following a three-year undergraduate or community college program. We are, therefore, advocating in this Bill dropping the lifetime limit of what students can borrow, which presently stands at $9,800, and replacing it by a simple limit of ten years. It has been generally agreed that dollar levels will be established which will be used as guidelines by Provinces to monitor the debt load of individual students.
The increase in loan limits to $100 a week will not satisfy- everyone, but in a time of economic restraint we had to look at a scale of assistance that we could deal with, thus the determination to see if we can help those who need help most.
This brings me to the second main concern with which we deal in this Bill, the client group served. The present Canada
Student Loans Program applies only to full-time students, but in today's society there is another population with very real needs as they pursue post-secondary education. I am referring to part-time students, both at universities and community colleges. This group of students has been making known its needs over the years. COPUS has made many representations. COPUS, the Canadian Organization of Part-Time University Students, represents over 250,000 students and as such reflects a real and growing constituency.
In recognizing the needs of part-time students we are recognizing the evolution of Canadian society. For instance, as women become a larger percentage of the labour force, parttime studies often provide them with a bridge between child rearing and employment. In many cases in the past, part-time students simply have not had the funds available to pursue the courses which could add to their future employability. This has meant a loss to the work force, particularly in regard to professional and skilled positions.
Under the Bill before the House, part-time students taking post-secondary courses accepted by the designated institution as credit toward a degree, diploma or certificate will qualify for a loan. There are, of course, various limitations to this provision. The course must be equivalent to a course that may be taken by a full-time student as part of a program of studies of at least 12 consecutive weeks' duration. The applicant must demonstrate a need for assistance as measured by a means test. The loan will cover the cost of tuition, books, transportation, child care and miscellaneous allowances.
At the present time it is difficult to predict how many part-time students would qualify for assistance under this new provision, but we anticipate that more than 20,000 to 30,000 students a year might apply.
The third main area of concern which we address in this Bill relates to the problems which many students are encountering when they complete their education and attempt to enter the labour force. The transition from university to the work place, which at one time could be accomplished within a space of one to four months, is no longer an easy transition.
As I see the clock, Mr. Speaker, I would like to stop at this point and resume the debate at two o'clock.
